Row.Text: The romance and drama of England’s medieval and early modern eras maintain a tight hold on the imagination of Western history. Between the 12th and 17th centuries, the kingdom dramatically evolved in the face of several repeating conflicts – the crown versus the church, the crown versus the barons, England versus France, England versus Britain’s Celtic populations – and underwent the fraught formation of English identity and the establishment of the groundwork for what would become the British Empire (our Great Britain in the Modern Age).

By the middle of the 12th century, foundations were laid for England’s next chapter by the Angevin branch of the Plantagenet kings – Henry II and his sons Richard I and John. Like their Norman predecessors, the Angevin monarchs were essentially French aristocrats who also happened to be kings of England. Their first language was French, followed by Latin, and John was the only one among them (and the first king since the Norman Conquest) who could speak English with any proficiency. Accordingly, their political focus was often on their French holdings rather than England.

Nonetheless, the 12th century was a period of significant change for England. Henry II (1154-1189) was an ambitious and tempestuous monarch, coming to power after a period of instability and civil crisis. His goal was to rebuild the kingdom as it was under his grandfather Henry I by centralizing power and expanding royal authority, and he largely succeeded. Yet his reign was also troubled by persistent strain between the crown and the church. The Catholic Church held immense power during the European Middle Ages as the one unifying entity across an otherwise fragmented continent, offering structure, community, and spiritual guidance to every level of society. It was one of two recognized and equal authorities in European kingdoms – the pope and clergy administered spiritual matters, while monarchs oversaw secular matters. However, the boundary between spiritual and secular authority was undefined, and attempts to reconcile these two sources of power often led to conflict. In England, this simmering tension was pervasive and age-defining, and it dramatically escalated during Henry II’s reign with the murder of Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, in 1170.

While Henry’s successor Richard I “the Lionheart” (1189-1199) has remained in the public imagination through Robin Hood narratives, it was his brother John (1199-1216) whose reign left a larger mark on history. Widely remembered as England’s worst monarch, he managed to lose almost all of England’s holdings in France early in his reign, fostering a rivalry between the two kingdoms that would spur many future wars. He also inherited the wrath of his nobility, whose frustration with the Angevin kings’ overreach of power had been brewing since Henry II’s reign. With the help of the church, the barons strong-armed John into signing the Magna Carta on June 15, 1215. This document laid out a wide variety of reforms to limit the king’s power and define protections for all free men. Although this first iteration of the Magna Carta was nullified by the pope only a few weeks later, resulting in the first of several civil wars between the barons and the crown, the document’s precedent has had significant impact through history, and its echoes resound in the Declaration of Independence and other key documents around the world.

As the Angevin era gave way to the later Plantagenet kings, the loss of French territories under John pushed England into a new phase – since the crown’s focus was now entirely on Britain, the boundaries between classes and cultures, once split between England and France, began to break down into a more cohesive English identity. Civil war between the barons and the crown carried through the 13th century, and a parliament was established in 1236. Tensions persisted with France and the Gaelic kingdoms, but things were about to get far, far worse.

England in the 14th century is defined by two catastrophic events. The first was the Hundred Years’ War, a series of conflicts between England and its old rival France. Their nuances are many, but the impact and results of these years of war were profound. The violence between the neighboring kingdoms further shaped English identity as the English came to define themselves in opposition to the French. The constant warfare also transformed military tactics, leading to the dominance of the longbow and the establishment of standing armies, which were easier to mobilize and maintain over long periods of conflict than seasonal levied forces.

The second catastrophe was the Black Death, the arrival of which resulted in the death of up to half of England’s population and dealt serious blows to the economy and social fabric. Among other shifts, the sudden and dramatic labor shortages led to the exploitation of the lower classes, which, combined with anger at excessive taxation to fund the Hundred Years’ War, eventually sparked revolt and the decline of serfdom in England a few decades later. These changes made space for the growing middle class and heralded the end of feudalism.

The Hundred Years’ War finally came to an end in 1453, and England immediately plunged into another conflict – the Wars of the Roses, a series of civil wars for the throne fought between two branches of the Plantagenet family. The victors were the Tudors, who would rule England until 1603. This period saw further major changes for England, including the English Reformation. Denied a divorce from his first wife by the pope, Henry VIII broke from the Catholic Church and started his own. A notable event in this process was the dissolution of England’s Catholic monasteries, whose land and assets were seized by Henry to fund his military campaigns. Monasteries were some of the largest landholders in England, and were major centers of learning and sources of charity; their dissolution left large gaps in social service, and the destruction of their libraries resulted in a loss of scholarship from the broader medieval period.

Medieval power in Europe often directly reflected the amount of land held by a kingdom. But as England, now diminished in size, entered the early modern period, it increasingly redefined its authority through its economy, which grew rapidly as lucrative trade networks migrated from the Mediterranean to the Baltic. Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries, England developed into a financial powerhouse, and enterprising joint-stock companies established footholds abroad. The North American colonies were soon followed by settlements in Asia and Africa, rapidly transforming the Kingdom of England into the British Empire.

The chapter house was the site of the abbey’s daily business, where all inhabitants came together to prepare for the day and handle institutional matters. A consistent feature of English monastic complexes (with rarer appearances on the continent), these spaces were ornate and lined with seats along the walls. Originally rectangular, they soon diversified in form, with the octagon proving particularly popular.

Morning assemblies began with the reading of a chapter from the monastic rule, from which the name “chapter house” derives. Names associated with the current date were read from the martyrology (a listing of saints) and the necrology (a listing of deceased members of the abbey and wider community). Finally, daily tasks were assigned among the monastics and disciplinary actions were carried out. Depending on the institution, additional meetings might take place later in the day.

As designated meeting spaces, chapter houses were also employed for political purposes. English monarchs used them to hold parliament and meet with dignitaries, and the House of Commons met in Westminster Abbey’s chapter house for several decades in the 14th century.

In Civilization VII, we have used “chapel” as a catch-all for the churches and cathedrals that were the centerpieces of English abbeys, priories, and monastic houses throughout the Middle Ages. These structures were immense undertakings, sometimes taking generations to construct, and by the 12th century promoted the Gothic architectural style that had rapidly spread from France. The combined innovations of the ribbed vault, pointed arch, and flying buttress allowed for higher and thinner walls and large stained-glass windows. The resulting structures were taller and lighter than ever before, and became increasingly ornate in the ensuing centuries, featuring complex vaulting, window tracery, and extensive sculpture.

Although primarily spaces for prayer and religious services, English chapels, churches, and cathedrals were also valuable sources of income for towns and monastic institutions. They housed saints’ relics that drew tourists, who purchased pilgrim badges and spent money in the surrounding community.

An abbey is a type of monastery following a particular religious order. Led by an abbot or abbess, the medieval English abbey was built around a church or cathedral, featuring the chapter house, refectory (the dining hall), cloister and garth (a central open-air courtyard), dormitories, library, and sometimes a scriptorium (where manuscripts were written and copied).

Abbeys were originally secluded, self-sufficient retreats for those wishing to devote their lives to the church. But they increasingly became institutions that also served the surrounding lay community through charity, religious service, education, and the production and sale of goods. As major landowners in England, abbeys profited greatly from the towns that grew up around them. The Reformation brought their age to a crashing end when Henry VIII violently shut down hundreds of monasteries, priories, and abbeys, seizing their assets and executing those who resisted.

Built in 1599 along the River Thames in London, the Globe Theatre was one of England’s most celebrated drama venues, made famous by its association with William Shakespeare. It was co-owned and operated by a combined group of investors and actors (including Shakespeare) and was designed as a space for audiences to witness and discuss contemporary issues through the lens of history, humanity, and, as indicated in the name, the world.

Although the exact design is unknown, the Globe is thought to have had three floors of galleries with an open yard for standing room and could have held up to 3,000 spectators. Many of Shakespeare’s most famous plays were staged here, and the theatre provided the playwright with the stability to fully indulge in his craft. Built cheaply of wood with a thatch roof, the theatre burned down in 1613 during a performance of “Henry VIII” when a cannon misfired. It was quickly rebuilt, the thatch replaced with tile, but was dismantled for tenements in 1644. A reconstruction of the Globe Theatre opened in 1997 next to its original site and remains a vibrant venue today.

The Angevin kings – Henry II, Richard I, and John – were the first branch of Plantagenet monarchs to take the throne of England. Predominantly French and named for the county of Anjou, they oversaw an empire that included both England and immense holdings in France.

Although sometimes playing second fiddle to the French territories, England underwent significant change under the Angevins that strengthened its position as a dominant power. As the shock of the Norman invasion wore off, royal power was consolidated and centralized, even as the church and the aristocracy became increasingly restive. England also underwent a major cultural shift during the renaissance of the 12th century, thriving on the rise and spread of education, scholarship, scientific innovation, and art, including the Gothic architectural style.

The Angevin era solidified the conflicts that would both plague and shape England for centuries to come. Internally, the crown and the church clashed over the bounds of their authority, culminating with the murder of Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, in 1170, while the crown and the barons quarreled over limitations on monarchical power, leading to the signing of the Magna Carta in 1215. Externally, the near total loss of French territories under John sparked a rivalry with France that would explode two centuries later into the Hundred Years’ War; and England’s subjugation of Britain’s Celtic populations began in earnest with Henry II’s conquest of Ireland in the late 12th century.

On October 31, 1517, Martin Luther nailed his Ninety-five Theses to the door of the church in Wittenberg, Germany, laying out a major theological challenge to the papacy. The resulting Reformation quickly spread across Europe, leading to the establishment of a new major branch of Christianity, Protestantism, and the opportunity to break away from the long-dominant Catholic Church.

Henry VIII of England saw other opportunities in this upheaval. Unable to produce a male heir with his wife Catherine of Aragon, he requested a divorce from the pope and was denied. Following the lessons of the Reformation, he subsequently founded his own Church of England, placed himself at its head, and approved his own divorce.

The English Reformation that followed had a profound impact on the kingdom beyond the royal lineage. Seeing financial opportunity, Henry dissolved all Catholic monastic institutions, seizing their assets, displacing thousands, and leaving ruins still visible in the landscape today. Later monarchs focused on theological and practical differences from Catholicism – English replaced Latin in both sermons and translations of the Bible, making services more accessible to the wider public, and altars and iconography were widely supplanted by new symbols and traditions. The English Reformation concluded under Elizabeth I with the establishment of the core of the Anglican Church, which remains the state church of England today.

As merchant adventurers established increasingly ambitious and profitable footholds overseas, the Board of Trade was founded as an advisory committee on matters of colonial governance and international trade. Often distracted by civil unrest in England, the committee’s rigor in tending to matters abroad varied widely, and the body itself underwent several iterations throughout the 16th century until the formal Board of Trade was established in 1696.

The committee was England’s attempt to harness its rapidly expanding overseas possessions under a single body to ensure both profitability and governmental oversight. The goal was ambitious, intended to tackle the challenges of a budding global empire head-on. However, the Board of Trade was ultimately too vulnerable to politics at home – its efficiency in overseeing the North American colonies in particular varied widely and often led to long periods of neglect before it was again temporarily abolished in 1782. Ironically, this neglect allowed the colonies additional freedom of self-governance, contributing to their path toward independence.
The Board of Trade has continued to phase in and out of British history and today acts as an advisory board on trade and the economy.

The expansion of English trade by the 15th century increasingly united merchants into companies to better organize, fund, and profit from overseas business. The earliest of these merchant adventurers specialized in the export of cloth to the Netherlands and Germany, often clashing with the Hanseatic League that had long dominated trade across Northern Europe. At their height, merchant adventurers controlled up to three-quarters of all foreign trade, and had significant influence at court, acting as financiers for the Tudor monarchs. Later ventures expanded English presence to more distant shores – Russia, the Middle East, the New World – building the infrastructure, both in colonies and trading companies, for the future British Empire.

The English longbow was a landmark weapon of the Middle Ages. Typically made of yew and averaging 6 to 7 feet in length, with a draw weight ranging from 80 to 150 pounds, the longbow could penetrate all but the heaviest steel plate and required constant lifelong training to achieve mastery. Its rise in medieval England was fueled by the widespread accessibility of bows (cheap enough to produce that anyone could own one) and the development of battlefield tactics that more efficiently deployed archery units. The zenith of the longbow’s fame came during the Hundred Years’ War, where it contributed to major English victories at Crécy, Poitiers, and Agincourt, among others.

By the 16th century, the longbow was phased out in favor of firearms – not because of inferiority (the longbow remained superior in many ways) but because of the excessive time and energy required to master the weapon.
